newsitem.title: SPAIN: After decades in spotlight, Gonzalez leaving stage.
newsitem.headline: After decades in spotlight, Gonzalez leaving stage.

text.p: Watching a new generation of Socialist leaders sweeping to power in Britain and France, former Spanish Prime Minister Felipe Gonzalez said recently he felt like a political "dinosaur."

Less than two weeks later, Gonzalez -- who persuaded Spain's socialist party to drop its Marxist label in the 1970s and has led it almost interrupted every since -- has apparently decided his time is up.

In a stunning display of political showmanship, he told the Socialist Workers' Party congress on Friday he would not seek re-election as secretary-general. "Please replace me," he urged, saying it was time for "a change of generations" in the party's leadership.
Gonzalez, who has grown weary of political life since Spanish voters pushed him out of office last year, has dominated his party like few other Western European politicians.

Not only has he never faced any serious opposition from within but he has never established a clear line of succession. As a result, his surprise announcement left the Socialists without any strong frontrunner to replace him.

And because brinkmanship has long been one of Gonzalez' trademarks, some party members were reluctant to rule out the possibility that he might have a change of heart and decide to remain party chief.
At age 55, Gonzalez -- the son of an Andalusian dairy farmer -- himself once represented a new generation in Spanish politics, those leaders born after the civil war.
He took over as secretary-general in 1974, winning election at a conference in France at a time when the party was still outlawed by the Spanish dictatorship of General Francisco Franco.
A natural politician and charismatic orator, Gonzalez succeeded in steering the party away from the radical left and adopting a more moderate strategy.
Gonzalez was 40 when his party first came to power in 1982 on a surge of popular support to rebuild Spain after nearly 40 years of authoritarian rule.

A former labour lawyer, Gonzalez and his equally young lieutenants consolidated Spain's young democracy, threw open the doors to the outside world and pursued free-market policies to launch an economic boom.
An anti-NATO activist when in the parliamentary opposition, he went on to lead Spain into the alliance and also gained membership of the European Union.
But Gonzalez was not without his critics.

Some accused him of squandering tax funds on glitzy events such as the Columbus quincentenary and the Barcelona Olympics in 1992. A few of old allies chided him for abandoning traditional socialist policies in favor of capitalism.
Spanish voters returned him to office three times, but in recent years a succession of corruption scandals eroded public confidence in Gonzalez and the socialist leadership.
In the most serious blow to Gonzalez' image, former security chiefs accused him of masterminding a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque separatist rebels in which 28 people were killed.
Gonzalez steadfastly denies the charges, but the scandal left a dark cloud over his 1996 re-election campaign. In the end, the Socialists were defeated by Jose Maria Aznar's Popular Party.

Since then, Gonzalez has continued to be dogged by "dirty war" allegations. Spain's Supreme Court voted last November against ordering Gonzalez to undergo questioning, and a lawyer for one of the victims' families said that would make him "the eternal suspect."
Despite that, Gonzalez has remained a popular figure, regularly edging out Prime Minister Aznar in opinion polls.

Gonzalez' decision to step down comes only weeks after socialists took power in Britain and France. He had reportedly been brooding about the decline in Spanish socialism, and politicians said he apparently determined that the only way to get his party to overhaul itself would be for him to stand aside.
"I am the dinosaur here," he said while attending a gathering of European socialists earlier this month in Sweden.
